questions.subject: bss
questions.q: O que é uma paisagem natural?
options: Uma paisagem só com ruas e carros
Uma paisagem quase sem mudanças feitas pelas pessoas
questions.answer: Uma paisagem quase sem mudanças feitas pelas pessoas
questions.hint: Pense no que existe antes de as pessoas construírem.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual destes lugares é um exemplo de paisagem natural?
questions.hint: Qual lugar não foi construído pelas pessoas?

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual destes elementos da paisagem foi feito pelas pessoas?
questions.hint: Três deles a natureza fez sozinha.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Como se chama a paisagem que foi transformada pelo trabalho das pessoas? Paisagem ___.
questions.hint: É o contrário de paisagem natural.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Uma praia com quiosques, calçadão e prédios na beira do mar é uma paisagem…
questions.hint: Veja se há coisas construídas.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Numa foto antiga de um bairro há chácaras e muitas árvores. Na foto atual há prédios e ruas asfaltadas. O que aconteceu com a paisagem?
questions.hint: Compare o que existia antes com o que existe agora.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual destas transformações acontece pela própria natureza, sem as pessoas?
options: Uma rocha se desgastar com a chuva e o vento
questions.answer: Uma rocha se desgastar com a chuva e o vento
questions.hint: Três delas precisam do trabalho humano.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual rio de São Paulo teve seu caminho alterado e hoje tem grandes avenidas nas margens, as Marginais?
questions.hint: É um rio que atravessa a cidade de São Paulo.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Antigamente, a Avenida Paulista tinha grandes casarões. O que existe hoje em grande parte dela?
options: Prédios altos de escritórios e lojas
questions.answer: Prédios altos de escritórios e lojas
questions.hint: Pense em como é uma avenida movimentada no centro de uma cidade grande.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Que meio de transporte circulava pelos trilhos das ruas de São Paulo antigamente e não circula mais hoje?
questions.hint: Ele andava sobre trilhos no meio da rua, puxado por energia elétrica.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Por que as pessoas modificam as paisagens?
options: Para mudar a cor do céu
Para construir casas, ruas e plantações
questions.answer: Para construir casas, ruas e plantações
questions.hint: Pense nas necessidades das pessoas que moram num lugar.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Ao comparar uma foto antiga e uma foto atual do mesmo lugar, observamos as permanências e as ___.
questions.hint: É o que ficou diferente de uma foto para a outra.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Uma área de mata foi derrubada para construir um bairro. O que pode acontecer?
options: Os animais perdem o lugar onde viviam
questions.answer: Os animais perdem o lugar onde viviam
questions.hint: Pense em quem morava na mata.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Um parque com lago artificial, caminhos de pedra e árvores plantadas é uma paisagem…
questions.hint: O lago e os caminhos foram feitos por quem?

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Pense na rua da sua casa ou da sua escola. Cite dois elementos naturais e dois elementos feitos pelas pessoas.
questions.hint: Árvores e céu são naturais; e o que foi construído?

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Você acha importante preservar algumas paisagens naturais? Explique por quê.
questions.hint: Pense nos animais, nas plantas e nas pessoas.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What is the main purpose of an explanation text?
options: To give instructions for a recipe
To explain how or why something happens
To persuade you to buy something
questions.answer: To explain how or why something happens
questions.hint: Think about the word 'explain'.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which is the best title for an explanation text?
questions.hint: Explanation titles often ask how or why.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Explanation texts about natural processes are usually written in which tense?
questions.hint: The process still happens today, again and again.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which conjunction shows cause and effect?
questions.hint: Which word tells you the reason something happens?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Choose the best causal conjunction: The puddle dries up ___ the sun heats the water.
questions.hint: The sun's heat is the reason the puddle dries.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: In the water cycle, what is it called when liquid water turns into water vapour?
questions.hint: It happens when the sun warms the sea.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What is the technical word for rain, snow, sleet or hail falling from clouds?
questions.hint: It is one of the main stages of the water cycle and starts with 'p'.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: When water vapour cools and turns back into tiny droplets that form clouds, this is called…
questions.hint: Think of the droplets on a cold window.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Water has collected in the sea. Which stage of the water cycle comes next?
questions.hint: The water must rise into the air first.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which sentence uses a time connective to show the order of a process?
options: Next, the water vapour rises into the sky.
questions.answer: Next, the water vapour rises into the sky.
questions.hint: Look for a word that tells you when.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which feature would you NOT normally find in an explanation text?
options: A title that asks a question
questions.hint: Explanation texts are non-fiction.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What is a glossary?
options: A list of technical words and their meanings
questions.answer: A list of technical words and their meanings
questions.hint: It helps readers understand difficult words.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which ending shows the effect? 'When the temperature drops below zero, ___'
questions.hint: What happens to water when it gets very cold?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which technical word names the hard case a caterpillar forms before it becomes a butterfly?
questions.hint: It starts with 'ch'.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which sentence would make the best final paragraph of an explanation about rain?
options: This is how water keeps moving around our planet, again and again.
Once upon a time there was a lonely cloud.
questions.answer: This is how water keeps moving around our planet, again and again.
questions.hint: A good ending sums up the process.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Write two sentences explaining what happens to a puddle on a hot day. Use 'because' or 'so'.
questions.hint: Think about what the sun does to the water.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: What is a journal?
options: A diary where someone writes what happens each day
questions.answer: A diary where someone writes what happens each day
questions.hint: Explorers write in one every evening.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: What is a biography?
options: A true account of a person's life written by someone else
A story a person writes about their own life
questions.answer: A true account of a person's life written by someone else
questions.hint: 'Bio' means life.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Journals are usually written in which person?
questions.hint: The writer is telling about their own day.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Read this journal entry: '3rd March 1852. We left the port of Kelmouth at dawn. The sea was calm.' On what date did the journey begin?
questions.hint: Look at the start of the entry.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Read: '10th April. After five weeks at sea, we finally saw land — a green island with tall cliffs.' What did the explorer see on 10th April?
options: A green island with tall cliffs
questions.answer: A green island with tall cliffs
questions.hint: Find the words after 'we finally saw land'.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Read: 'Born in 1820 in a small fishing village, Ada Thorne dreamed of the frozen north.' Where was Ada Thorne born?
questions.hint: Look for the place in the sentence.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Read: 'Tomas Rell was born in 1790. He reached the great mountain pass in 1823.' How old was he when he reached the pass?
questions.hint: Subtract the year he was born from the year he reached the pass.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Read: 'In 1838, Ada joined a whaling ship as a cook. In 1848, she led her own expedition. In 1845, she learnt to navigate by the stars.' Which event happened second?
options: She learnt to navigate by the stars
She joined a whaling ship as a cook
questions.answer: She learnt to navigate by the stars
questions.hint: Put the years in order from earliest to latest.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Which word in this sentence signals time? 'Eventually, he returned home.'
questions.hint: Which word tells you when?

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Read: 'Day 12. Snow again. Our food is running low and the dogs are tired.' How do you think the explorer feels?
questions.hint: Think about having little food in the snow.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Read: 'We crossed the River Senna on 2nd June and reached the village of Orlo two days later.' On what date did they reach Orlo?
questions.hint: Count two days on from 2nd June.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Why do explorers keep journals?
options: To tell jokes to the crew
To record what they see and do each day
questions.answer: To record what they see and do each day
questions.hint: Think about remembering a long journey.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Which sentence is most likely from a biography, not a journal?
options: She was born in a cold northern town in 1801.
Today I saw a whale beside our ship!
questions.answer: She was born in a cold northern town in 1801.
questions.hint: A biography uses 'he' or 'she'.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: What is chronological order?
options: The order in which events happened
questions.answer: The order in which events happened
questions.hint: 'Chrono' is about time.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Read: 'Before setting off, Mira Kade spent a year studying maps. During the voyage she discovered a hidden bay. After returning home, she wrote a book.' What did Mira do after returning home?
questions.hint: Find the words 'after returning home'.

questions.subject: en_read
questions.q: Would you rather read an explorer's journal or a biography about them? Give one reason.
questions.hint: Think about whose voice you would hear.

ipc.topic: Explorers and Adventurers: why do people explore?

questions.subject: ipc
questions.q: What is an explorer?
options: A person who travels to discover new places
A person who only stays at home
questions.answer: A person who travels to discover new places
questions.hint: Think about the word 'explore'.

questions.subject: ipc
questions.q: Which of these is a reason people explored in the past?
options: To find new places to trade goods
questions.answer: To find new places to trade goods
questions.hint: Long ago, people wanted spices, silk and gold.

questions.subject: ipc
questions.q: What word means 'buying, selling or swapping goods'?
questions.hint: Merchants did this at markets and ports.

questions.subject: ipc
questions.q: What word means 'a strong wish to know or learn something'?
questions.hint: It comes from the word 'curious'.

questions.subject: ipc
questions.q: Which quality helps an explorer keep going when a journey gets hard?
questions.hint: It means not giving up.

questions.subject: ipc
questions.q: Which tool did sailors long ago use to find which direction was north?
questions.hint: Its needle is magnetic.

questions.subject: ipc
questions.q: Some explorers wanted fame. What does 'fame' mean?
options: Being known by lots of people
questions.answer: Being known by lots of people

questions.subject: ipc
questions.q: Which of these was a big danger for sailors on very long sea voyages long ago?

getting lost in a shopping centre

questions.subject: ipc
questions.q: What do we call the record an explorer writes each day about their journey? (one word)

questions.subject: ipc
questions.q: Why do modern explorers go to the deep ocean or to space?
options: To learn new things through science

questions.subject: ipc
questions.q: Which continent is covered in ice and was one of the last to be explored?

questions.subject: ipc
questions.q: Which quality means being ready to face danger even when you feel scared?

questions.subject: ipc
questions.q: Why did explorers need maps?
options: To plan routes and record where they had been
questions.answer: To plan routes and record where they had been

questions.subject: ipc
questions.q: Which of these is NOT a good quality for an explorer?

questions.subject: ipc

questions.hint: Think about what the explorer hoped to gain.

options: Com um pequeno espaço da margem e letra maiúscula
Com letra minúscula colada na margem
questions.answer: Com um pequeno espaço da margem e letra maiúscula
questions.hint: Olhe o começo dos parágrafos num livro.

questions.q: Como se chama o pequeno espaço deixado no começo de cada parágrafo? (uma palavra)

questions.hint: Imagine ler uma página inteira sem pausas.

chapters.title: Capítulo 1: O canto no rio
chapters.synopsis: Lia e Davi viajam de barco pela Amazônia com a Tia Rosa e ouvem do barqueiro a lenda da Iara. À noite, um som bonito no rio deixa Davi assustado, mas tem uma explicação.
chapters.text:
Lia tinha nove anos e um caderno de capa verde onde anotava tudo. O irmão, Davi, tinha oito e não largava a lanterna. Naquelas férias, os dois foram viajar com a Tia Rosa, que era contadora de histórias e queria recolher lendas de diferentes regiões do Brasil.
A primeira parada foi a Amazônia. Eles subiram num barco de madeira que descia um rio largo e escuro, com a floresta dos dois lados. O barqueiro, seu Dico, tinha mãos fortes e uma risada que ecoava na água.
— Vocês já ouviram falar da Iara? — perguntou ele, quando o sol começou a se pôr.
As crianças balançaram a cabeça. Seu Dico contou que a Iara era a Mãe-d'Água, uma moça muito bonita, metade mulher e metade peixe, com cabelos longos e escuros. Ela vivia no fundo dos rios e, no fim da tarde, sentava numa pedra para pentear os cabelos e cantar.
— O canto dela é tão lindo que os pescadores ficam encantados — explicou ele. — Quem segue a voz é levado para o fundo do rio e nunca mais volta.
Lia anotou tudo no caderno: "Iara — Região Norte — vive nos rios — metade mulher, metade peixe — encanta com o canto."
Naquela noite, deitado na rede, Davi ouviu um som fino e bonito vindo da água. Ele apertou a lanterna e acordou a irmã.
— Lia! É a Iara cantando!
Os dois foram até a beira do barco, devagar. Davi apontou a lanterna para o rio. Lá estava seu Dico, sentado na proa, tocando uma flauta de bambu.
— Desculpem — riu o barqueiro. — Toco para espantar o sono.
Davi ficou vermelho, mas depois riu também. Antes de dormir, Lia escreveu mais uma linha: "Às vezes, um som de verdade faz a gente lembrar de uma lenda."

chapters.title: Capítulo 2: O rapaz de chapéu branco
chapters.synopsis: Numa festa da comunidade ribeirinha, as crianças ouvem a lenda do Boto e desconfiam de um moço de roupa branca e chapéu. No fim, descobrem quem ele é.
chapters.text:
No dia seguinte, o barco parou numa comunidade ribeirinha, com casas de madeira sobre palafitas. Era noite de festa: havia fogueira, bandeirinhas e um forró animado num barracão perto do rio.
Dona Benta Maria, uma senhora de tranças brancas, sentou ao lado das crianças e contou a lenda do Boto.
— O boto-cor-de-rosa vive nos rios da Amazônia. Mas, em noite de festa, ele sai da água e vira um rapaz elegante, todo de branco, com um chapéu na cabeça.
— Por que o chapéu? — perguntou Davi.
— Para esconder o furinho que o boto tem no alto da cabeça, por onde respira — explicou ela. — Ele dança muito bem, encanta as moças e, antes de o sol nascer, volta correndo para o rio e vira boto de novo.
Lia escreveu depressa: "Boto — Região Norte — vive nos rios — vira rapaz de branco — encanta dançando — nunca tira o chapéu."
Pouco depois, entrou no barracão um moço de camisa branca e chapéu de palha claro. Dançava tão bem que todo mundo abriu roda. Davi cutucou a irmã.
— É ele! E não tira o chapéu!
As crianças passaram a festa vigiando o moço. Quando a música parou, ele subiu no palco e pegou uma sanfona. Então tirou o chapéu para enxugar a testa. Não havia furinho nenhum, só um cabelo todo bagunçado.
— Boa noite! Eu sou o Joca, o sanfoneiro! — disse ele, e a festa recomeçou.
Tia Rosa riu e explicou que muitas pessoas da região se vestem de branco nas festas por causa do calor. Lia fechou o caderno, satisfeita. Agora tinha duas lendas das águas, e uma ideia começava a nascer na cabeça dela.

chapters.title: Capítulo 3: A tabela das águas
chapters.synopsis: Lia monta no caderno uma tabela para comparar a Iara e o Boto. Ela e Davi descobrem semelhanças e diferenças entre os dois seres lendários.
chapters.text:
Na viagem de volta pelo rio, choveu a manhã inteira. Sem poder ficar na proa, Lia abriu o caderno verde em cima de um caixote e desenhou uma tabela com três colunas: "O que comparar", "Iara" e "Boto".
— Para que isso? — perguntou Davi, bocejando.
— Para ver no que eles são parecidos e no que são diferentes — respondeu ela. — A Tia Rosa disse que comparar ajuda a entender as lendas.
Os dois começaram pela primeira linha: "Onde vive". Nas duas colunas, Lia escreveu "nos rios da Amazônia".
— Igual! — disse Davi, já interessado.
Na linha "Como é", a resposta mudou. A Iara era metade mulher e metade peixe. O Boto era um animal de verdade, o boto-cor-de-rosa, que virava um rapaz.
— Então a Iara é sempre meio peixe, e o Boto muda de forma — concluiu Davi.
Na linha "Como encanta as pessoas", Lia pensou um pouco. A Iara encantava com o canto. O Boto encantava dançando nas festas.
— Os dois encantam, mas de jeitos diferentes — disse ela, sublinhando a palavra "encantam".
Por último, a linha "Quando aparece". A Iara cantava no fim da tarde, sentada numa pedra. O Boto aparecia em noites de festa e sumia antes do amanhecer.
Tia Rosa espiou por cima do ombro da sobrinha e sorriu.
— Vocês descobriram uma coisa importante. Muitas lendas da Amazônia falam dos rios, porque o rio é o centro da vida das pessoas de lá: é estrada, é comida, é casa.
Davi olhou para a água barrenta lá fora. De repente, o rio parecia ainda maior e mais cheio de segredos. Lia deixou duas linhas em branco no fim da tabela. Ainda faltava uma lenda, e ela vinha de bem longe dali.

chapters.title: Capítulo 4: A lenda que galopa
chapters.synopsis: A viagem continua num sítio do interior do Sudeste, onde Vô Tonico conta a lenda da Mula sem cabeça. As crianças percebem que ela é bem diferente das lendas das águas.
chapters.text:
Depois da Amazônia, Tia Rosa levou as crianças para um sítio no interior de Minas Gerais. Ali não havia rio largo, e sim morros, pastos, um curral e uma igrejinha branca lá no alto.
O dono do sítio era o Vô Tonico, um senhor de bigode grosso que fazia o melhor pão de queijo do mundo, segundo Davi. Depois do jantar, com todos em volta do fogão a lenha, ele baixou a voz.
— Aqui no interior, a lenda mais conhecida é a da Mula sem cabeça.
Davi chegou mais perto da irmã.
— Dizem que ela era uma mulher que recebeu um castigo e virou uma mula — continuou o avô. — No lugar da cabeça, sai fogo do pescoço. Ela galopa pelos campos nas noites de quinta para sexta-feira, e as ferraduras fazem um barulho de metal que assusta todo mundo.
— E dá para parar ela? — perguntou Lia.
— Contam que, se alguém tirar o freio de ferro que ela usa, o encanto se quebra e ela volta a ser gente.
Lia abriu o caderno na tabela e escreveu uma nova coluna: "Mula sem cabeça — Sudeste e outras regiões — vive nos campos — mula com fogo no lugar da cabeça — assusta, não encanta — noite de quinta para sexta."
— Essa é bem diferente — comentou ela. — A Iara e o Boto atraem as pessoas. A Mula faz todo mundo fugir.
— E elas são da água, e essa é da terra — completou Davi.
Tia Rosa piscou para os dois.
— Repararam no dia de hoje?
As crianças olharam o calendário pendurado na parede da cozinha. Era quinta-feira. Lá fora, o vento balançava as árvores, e Davi decidiu que dormiria com a lanterna acesa.

chapters.title: Capítulo 5: Barulho de cascos
chapters.synopsis: Na noite de quinta-feira, as crianças ouvem cascos de metal no pasto. Com a ajuda do Vô Tonico, descobrem que é a égua Estrela, que fugiu do curral.
chapters.text:
Já passava da meia-noite quando Davi acordou com um barulho lá fora: tlec, tlec, tlec. Era som de cascos batendo nas pedras do caminho, com um tilintar de metal.
— Lia! — sussurrou ele. — A Mula sem cabeça!
Lia sentou na cama com o coração aos pulos. O barulho passou perto da janela e foi na direção do pasto. Ela respirou fundo e lembrou de uma coisa que a Tia Rosa sempre dizia: "Primeiro a gente observa, depois a gente conclui."
— Vamos olhar pela janela. Só olhar — decidiu ela.
Davi acendeu a lanterna e apontou para fora. A luz mostrou um vulto grande andando no escuro. Tinha patas, rabo... e cabeça! Uma cabeça com uma mancha branca bem no meio da testa.
— Tem cabeça — disse Lia, aliviada. — E não tem fogo nenhum.
Nesse momento, a porta da cozinha rangeu. Era o Vô Tonico, de chinelo e casaco por cima do pijama, segurando um lampião.
— Ouvi a Estrela — resmungou ele. — Essa égua aprendeu a abrir a porteira do curral com o focinho!
As crianças pediram para ajudar. Vestiram os casacos e seguiram o avô até o pasto. Davi iluminava o caminho, e Lia segurava um balde de milho. Quando a égua ouviu o milho chacoalhar, veio trotando, e as ferraduras fizeram de novo aquele som de metal.
— Foi esse o barulho que vocês ouviram — explicou o avô, rindo. — Ferradura em pedra.
De volta para a cama, Davi estava orgulhoso de ter ajudado. Lia abriu o caderno e escreveu: "A lenda fala de ferraduras e de noite escura. Talvez as pessoas antigas também ouvissem cavalos no escuro e imaginassem coisas." Depois apagou a luz e dormiu sem medo.

chapters.title: Capítulo 6: O cartaz das três lendas
chapters.synopsis: De volta à cidade, Lia e Davi preparam um cartaz para a feira de cultura da escola. Eles organizam as comparações e discutem como apresentar cada lenda.
chapters.text:
Quando as férias acabaram, a professora Marta anunciou a Feira de Cultura Brasileira. Cada dupla apresentaria um trabalho sobre o folclore. Lia e Davi estudavam na mesma escola e pediram para fazer juntos.
— Já temos tudo no caderno verde! — disse Lia.
Num sábado, espalharam uma cartolina enorme no chão da sala. Lia queria fazer uma tabela grande, igual à do caderno. Davi queria desenhar os três seres lendários bem coloridos.
— Por que não os dois? — sugeriu Tia Rosa, que tinha vindo ajudar.
Eles dividiram a cartolina. Em cima, Davi desenhou a Iara numa pedra, penteando os cabelos; o Boto de chapéu branco, dançando; e a Mula sem cabeça galopando, com fogo saindo do pescoço. Embaixo, Lia fez a tabela com as linhas "Onde vive", "Região", "Como é", "O que faz" e "Quando aparece".
Enquanto pintava, Davi parou de repente.
— Lia, e se a gente colocar uma linha "Atrai ou assusta?"
— Boa! — respondeu ela. — A Iara atrai, o Boto atrai e a Mula assusta.
Tia Rosa sugeriu mais uma coisa: um cantinho chamado "O que essas lendas ensinam". As crianças pensaram juntas. A Iara e o Boto lembravam que o rio pode ser perigoso e que é preciso respeitar a água. A Mula sem cabeça fazia as crianças do interior voltarem cedo para casa e não andarem sozinhas pelos campos à noite.
— As lendas são como conselhos contados de um jeito divertido — resumiu Tia Rosa.
No fim da tarde, o cartaz estava pronto. Davi colou uma ferradura de papel prateado no canto, e Lia colou uma pequena flauta de papel, em homenagem ao seu Dico. Os dois olharam o trabalho, orgulhosos. Só faltava uma coisa: ensaiar a apresentação, e Davi tremia só de pensar em falar na frente da turma.

chapters.title: Capítulo 7: A lenda do caderno verde
chapters.synopsis: Na Feira de Cultura, Davi vence o nervosismo e apresenta o cartaz com Lia. No final, a turma inventa junto uma lenda nova.
chapters.text:
No dia da feira, o pátio da escola estava cheio de cartazes, fantasias e cheiro de pipoca. Lia e Davi colocaram o cartaz num cavalete e esperaram a vez deles. Davi suava frio.
— E se eu esquecer tudo? — cochichou ele.
— Você não vai esquecer. Você viveu tudo isso — respondeu Lia. — É só contar como aconteceu.
Quando a professora Marta chamou, Lia começou explicando a tabela. Mostrou que a Iara e o Boto são lendas da Região Norte, ligadas aos rios, e que a Mula sem cabeça é contada no interior de várias regiões, ligada aos campos.
Então foi a vez de Davi. Ele olhou para a turma, respirou fundo e contou a história da flauta de seu Dico, do moço de chapéu branco que era sanfoneiro e da égua Estrela galopando no escuro. A turma riu nas partes certas e ficou em silêncio nas partes de suspense. Davi nem percebeu que o nervosismo tinha ido embora.
— Então vocês acham que as lendas não existem? — perguntou um colega, o Rafa.
Davi pensou um pouco.
— Acho que os seres não existem, mas as lendas existem, sim. Elas fazem parte da cultura do Brasil e mostram como as pessoas de cada lugar vivem e o que elas temem.
A professora gostou tanto da resposta que propôs uma brincadeira: a turma inteira ia inventar uma lenda nova, sobre a própria escola. Em poucos minutos nasceu o "Guardião do Caderno Verde", um ser que vive na biblioteca, tem asas de papel e só aparece para quem anota as histórias que ouve.
Na volta para casa, Tia Rosa abraçou os sobrinhos.
— Agora vocês também são contadores de histórias.
Naquela noite, Lia abriu o caderno numa página nova e escreveu o título com letras caprichadas: "Próxima viagem: lendas do Sul." Davi, ao lado, já estava separando a lanterna.

books.title: The Journals of Captain Ada Finch
books.premise: Milo and his grandad discover the old journals of Captain Ada Finch, a sea explorer from their small town, and read one every Saturday, using her dates and places to piece together her voyage to the icy Whitecap Islands and the story of her whole life.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Tin Box
chapters.synopsis: Milo and his grandad find an old tin box of journals at the town museum and learn who wrote them: an explorer called Captain Ada Finch.
chapters.text:
On a wet Saturday in October, Milo helped his grandad tidy the back room of the Harrowby Town Museum. Grandad had looked after the museum for twenty years, and he said there were still boxes nobody had opened.
Behind a pile of old fishing nets, Milo found a tin box painted dark green. The lid was stiff with rust. When Grandad finally prised it open, they saw five small notebooks tied with string, a brass compass and a faded photograph of a woman in a thick coat standing on the deck of a ship.
"Well, I never," said Grandad, peering at the first page. "These belong to Captain Ada Finch."
Milo had seen that name on a plaque by the harbour, but he had never known who she was. Grandad pulled up two chairs and explained.
"Ada Finch was born here in Harrowby on 12th May 1868. Her father was a fisherman, and she learned to read the tides before she could ride a bicycle. When she was seventeen, in 1885, she went to sea for the first time as a ship's cook. Twenty years later, she was captain of her own ship, the Kestrel."
"And these are her journals?" Milo asked.
"Explorers wrote everything down," said Grandad. "Dates, places, the weather, what they ate. A journal was their memory. Without it, nobody back home would ever know what they had seen."
Milo opened the first notebook carefully. The ink was brown and the writing was small and neat. At the top of the page it said: 3rd March 1906, Port Merrow.
"Can we read them?" he asked.
Grandad smiled. "One journal every Saturday. That way we'll make them last."
Milo put the compass in his pocket for safekeeping, and for the first time he could remember, he couldn't wait for next Saturday.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Leaving Port Merrow
chapters.synopsis: The first journal describes the Kestrel setting sail from Port Merrow in March 1906 and a frightening storm on the fourth day.
chapters.text:
The next Saturday, Milo and Grandad sat by the museum window and read the first journal aloud, taking turns.
"3rd March 1906, Port Merrow. Cold and bright. We have loaded forty barrels of fresh water, salted fish, oats, and enough lamp oil for three months. My crew is eleven people, and every one of them has sailed with me before. Our aim is to reach the Whitecap Islands in the far north and draw the first true map of their coast."
Milo stopped. "The first true map? Didn't anyone know what they looked like?"
"Only roughly," said Grandad. "Sailors had seen them from far away. Nobody had walked along the shore and measured it."
Milo read on. "4th March 1906. We left the harbour at dawn with the tide. The whole town came to wave. My mother gave me a jar of plum jam and told me to come home thinner but wiser."
Grandad laughed. "That sounds like a Harrowby mother."
The next entries were short: good wind, a pod of whales, a seagull that stole a biscuit from the cook. Then the handwriting changed. It was bigger and rushed, as if the pen had been shaking.
"7th March 1906. Storm since midnight. Waves taller than the mast. We tied ourselves to the rails so that nobody would be washed overboard. The young sailor Tobias was sick all night, but he never let go of the rope. By noon the wind dropped. We have lost two barrels of water but no people. I thank the sea for that."
Milo looked up. "She thanked the sea? Even after it nearly sank them?"
"Explorers respected the sea," said Grandad. "It could carry them or it could swallow them. Ada knew that better than most."
Milo copied the three dates into his own notebook: 3rd March, 4th March, 7th March. He was beginning to feel like an explorer himself.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Whitecap Islands
chapters.synopsis: Ada reaches the Whitecap Islands and begins mapping the coast, with Milo using her dates to work out how long the journey took.
chapters.text:
The second journal had a picture of a mountain glued inside the cover, drawn in pencil. Underneath, Ada had written: The view from the ship, 19th March 1906.
"19th March 1906. Land! At first light, the lookout shouted from the top of the mast. Three islands, white with snow, rising out of a grey sea. The tallest peak I have named Mount Merrow, after our home port. The air smells of ice and salt."
"How long did it take them to get there?" asked Grandad, with a twinkle in his eye.
Milo checked his notebook. "They left on the 4th of March and saw land on the 19th. So… fifteen days."
"Spot on. You're reading like a real historian."
Milo turned the page. "21st March 1906. We rowed ashore at a small bay with black stones. I have called it Kettle Bay because the steam from our cooking pot was the only warm thing for miles. We set up two tents and a flagpole. Tomorrow we begin to measure the coast."
The entries after that were full of numbers. Ada and her crew walked along the shore every day with a long chain to measure distances. Each evening she drew what they had measured. A small sketch of the coastline grew a little bigger on every page, like a puzzle being finished piece by piece.
"30th March 1906. Nine days of measuring. Fourteen miles of coast drawn. Tobias found a nest of eider ducks and did not take a single egg, because I told him the mothers needed them more than we did. He is becoming a good explorer."
Milo traced the little map with his finger. "She was really patient."
"Mapping is slow work," said Grandad. "But a good map can keep sailors safe for a hundred years."
Milo noticed that Ada's handwriting was neat again. The storm was far behind them now.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Missing Page
chapters.synopsis: Milo discovers that a page is missing from the third journal and uses the dates around it to work out what might have happened.
chapters.text:
The third journal began cheerfully. "2nd April 1906. Sunshine at last. We reached the second island by rowing boat and found hot springs bubbling between the rocks. The crew took turns warming their feet."
Milo read on happily until he turned a page and stopped. "Grandad, there's a page missing."
Grandad leaned over. Someone had torn a page out neatly, close to the stitching. The entry before it was dated 5th April. The entry after it was dated 9th April.
"So we don't know what happened on the 6th, 7th and 8th," Milo said. "That's three whole days."
"Then let's be detectives," said Grandad. "What clues does the next entry give us?"
Milo read slowly. "9th April 1906. Back at Kettle Bay. Tobias's ankle is strapped and he is cross about it. We will not try the ice bridge again. I have marked it on the map as DANGER, and I hope every captain who reads this map will listen."
Milo thought hard. "An ice bridge... a strapped ankle... a danger sign. I think they tried to cross some ice, and Tobias slipped and hurt his foot."
"That's a good inference," said Grandad. "You used the clues on the page to work out something the writer didn't tell us directly."
"But why would Ada tear the page out?"
Grandad shrugged. "Perhaps she wrote it in a panic and was embarrassed later. Perhaps the page got wet and she threw it away. We may never know for sure. Historians have to be honest about what they don't know."
Milo found the map in the back of the journal. On a narrow strip between two islands, in red ink, was the word DANGER and a tiny drawing of a cracked line.
He wrote in his notebook: 6th to 8th April: missing. Probably an accident on the ice bridge. Then he added one more word: probably. A good detective, he decided, was careful with that word.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: The Long Way Home
chapters.synopsis: The fourth journal follows the Kestrel home in May 1906, including a surprise visit to a fishing village where Ada swaps maps for food.
chapters.text:
"This one's thinner," said Milo, holding up the fourth journal. "Maybe they were too tired to write much."
"Or they were too busy sailing," said Grandad. "Let's see."
"1st May 1906. The map of the Whitecap coast is finished: thirty-one miles, three islands, nine bays. We sail for home tomorrow. The crew sang all evening. Tobias, who can now walk without a stick, sang loudest."
Milo grinned. He was glad Tobias's ankle had healed.
"2nd May 1906. Left Kettle Bay. I looked back until Mount Merrow was only a white dot."
The next entries described fog so thick that the crew could not see the front of their own ship, and a week of calm when there was no wind at all. Food began to run low. Then came a happier entry.
"14th May 1906. We anchored at the fishing village of Sallowmouth. The people here had never seen a ship from so far south. I traded a copy of our new map for fresh bread, eggs and a sack of potatoes. The headwoman said the map would help their boats avoid the rocks near the islands. It is the best trade I have ever made."
"She gave away her map?" Milo asked, surprised. "After all that work?"
"A copy," said Grandad. "And think about it. What good is a map if it stays in a drawer? Ada wanted it to be useful."
Milo nodded slowly. He flipped forward. "20th May 1906. Harrowby in sight. Someone on the harbour wall is waving a red scarf. I think it is my mother."
Milo closed the journal and counted on his fingers. "They left on the 4th of March and got home on the 20th of May. That's about two and a half months away."
"Eleven weeks," said Grandad. "And every day written down."
Milo looked at the brass compass on the table. It suddenly felt much heavier, full of all those miles.

chapters.title: Chapter 6: The Last Journal
chapters.synopsis: The final journal is different: it is written years later, when Ada is older, and tells what she did with the rest of her life.
chapters.text:
The fifth journal had a blue cover instead of a brown one, and the writing inside was shakier.
"This was written much later," said Grandad, pointing to the first date. "Look: 1st January 1930."
Milo did the sum in his head. "If she was born in 1868, she was sixty-one, nearly sixty-two."
"Exactly. Let's hear what she says."
"1st January 1930. A new year, and I am an old woman with too many memories and not enough shelves. My granddaughter asked me today to tell her the story of my life in order, from the beginning. So I shall write it here, simply, so that it does not get muddled."
What followed was a list. Milo read it slowly, and Grandad wrote each line on a sheet of paper.
"1868: born in Harrowby. 1885: first went to sea as a cook. 1898: became first mate, the second in command. 1905: became captain of the Kestrel. 1906: mapped the Whitecap Islands. 1912: taught navigation at the harbour school. 1924: gave the Kestrel to the town as a training ship for young sailors."
"She taught other people," said Milo. "So they could be explorers too."
"That's right. And the Kestrel trained sailors for many years after that."
The last entry in the journal was short.
"I have one wish left. I would like the town to keep a small museum, so that children can see that people from a little place like Harrowby can go a very long way."
Milo looked around the room: the fishing nets, the dusty glass cases, the old photographs on the walls. Then he looked at Grandad.
"Is that why this museum exists?"
Grandad nodded. "It opened in 1931, a year after she wrote that. Ada didn't live to see the opening day, but her granddaughter cut the ribbon."
Milo was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "We should finish what she started."

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Ada Finch Day
chapters.synopsis: Milo uses everything he has learned to make a timeline of Ada's life for a new museum display, which opens on her birthday.
chapters.text:
For the next three weeks, Milo spent every Saturday at the museum. He and Grandad cleared out a glass case near the front door, polished the brass compass until it shone and pinned the faded photograph of Ada on a dark green board.
"Every good display tells a story," said Grandad. "What story do you want to tell?"
Milo knew straight away. "Her life, in order. A timeline. Then anyone can follow it, even little children."
He cut a long strip of card and drew a line across it. At the left end he wrote 1868 and at the right end 1931. Then, using his notebook and Ada's own list, he added every important event in the right place: her birth, her first voyage as a cook, becoming first mate, becoming captain, the Whitecap voyage, teaching at the harbour school, giving away the Kestrel and the opening of the museum.
Under 1906, he added a small box with extra details from the journals: Left Port Merrow 4th March. Storm 7th March. Saw land 19th March. Home 20th May.
"You've used her journals like a real biographer," said Grandad. "A biographer is someone who writes the true story of another person's life."
"I left the missing page as a question mark," Milo said. "Because we don't really know."
"That," said Grandad, "is the most honest thing on the whole board."
They opened the new display on 12th May, Ada's birthday. Children from Milo's school came, and so did people from the harbour. A girl in Year 2 asked who Tobias was. An old fisherman said his grandfather had trained on the Kestrel.
At the end of the day, Grandad handed Milo the green tin box. It was empty now, but it was clean, and the lid opened easily.
"What's this for?" Milo asked.
"For your journals," said Grandad. "Every explorer needs one."
That night, Milo wrote his first entry: 12th May. Harrowby. Today I told someone's story. Tomorrow, I start my own.
